answer:
**Yes, potentially—but only indirectly.** If the fund has the required SEC relief permitting ETF and mutual-fund classes to share one portfolio, ETF redemptions in kind can transfer appreciated securities out of the RIC rather than sell them. Under the tax rules for RICs, a qualifying in-kind redemption generally does not make the fund recognize gain on those securities. That can reduce portfolio-wide realized gains and taxable distributions, benefiting mutual-fund shareholders as well as ETF holders.

The benefit is not guaranteed or exclusive to the mutual-fund class: it depends on actual in-kind redemptions, the securities and tax lots delivered, and the fund’s trading and distribution needs. Redemptions can also affect portfolio composition and transaction costs.

Crucially, **RIC status alone does not authorize a shared ETF/mutual-fund portfolio or establish this treatment in every structure.** The fund must have applicable SEC share-class relief and comply with its conditions; absent that relief, the classes generally cannot simply share a portfolio. Tax treatment also depends on the transaction meeting applicable requirements, so this is not a promise of tax-free investor outcomes.
